title: The Making of Crime Predictions: Sociotechnical Assemblages and the Controversies of Governing Future Crime
thesis: Traces the sociotechnical assemblage of CrimeRadar to show how political choices and biases are embedded in algorithmic crime forecasts, challenging claims of objectivity.
theme_1_justification: Not addressed. No discussion of dual-use, technology transfer, or information good properties.
theme_2_justification: Central argument. Extensively discusses algorithmic opacity (black boxes), epistemic authority of data-driven systems, naturalization of political choices, and democratic deficit in predictive policing.
theme_3_justification: Tangential mention. References 'algorithmic turn in governance' and 'actuarial justice' but does not develop machinic city or modulation concepts.
theme_4_justification: Not addressed. No discussion of spatial destruction, urbicide, or weaponisation of urban data.
key_quotes: As often happens with big data and machine-learning innovations, automated decisions with deep influence in society are made by algorithms hidden in black boxes (Pasquale 2015).

the algorithm itself is powered by 'concrete data, and its mathematics has no bias.... If a crime happened, the algorithm will see it, will read it without putting human values, and will make a prediction based on that. So, it's certainly impartial'.
the multiple choices involved in these practices are naturalized and de-politicized in the process of translating crime events into strings of codes, datasets, and maps.
notes: Full text provided. Journal article in Surveillance & Society.
